kurz: Water only boils at 100 °C at sea level. In the mountains it boils sooner; in a pressure cooker only at about 120 °C.
bild_im_kopf: Like a lid on a packed hall: if it presses down hard, nobody gets out until it gets really hot.
was_passiert: [[wasser|Water]] boils when its vapour pushes as hard as the air above it. Lower air pressure at altitude means it boils at a lower [[temperatur|temperature]], about 1 °C less for every 300 metres. At 3000 m water boils at around 90 °C. A pressure cooker does the opposite: it holds the steam back, the pressure rises, and water gets about 120 °C hot. Higher temperature means shorter cooking time.
warum_wichtig: Explains why pasta and eggs take longer in a mountain hut, and why a pressure cooker cooks beans and braising meat in a fraction of the time.
faustregeln: In the mountains, extend cooking times. More heat does not help: water there gets no hotter than its boiling point.
Pressure cooker for pulses, stock and braises: about a third of the time.
Open a pressure cooker only once the pressure has fully dropped.

praxis.text: A 6-minute egg at 2000 m is softer than in the lowlands, because the water boils cooler.
Braised beef in a pressure cooker turns tender in around an hour.
